<reason>Both sides fought the right clash: PRO framed the motion as comparative ("name a better achievable rival"), CON correctly seized on "achievable." CON's strongest work was the mechanism squeeze — PRO's own answer conceded a package "no coalition has yet been offered," a bloc-swap map Palestinians rejected three times, and removal of "tens of thousands" of the most ideological settlers — plus the sharp turnaround on coercion ("who removes the settler in Kiryat Arba? The IDF, ten times over"). But CON's route to victory depended entirely on a stipulated definition that "two-state solution" means hard territorial separation, and PRO attacked that hinge early and never let go: a confederation of Israel and Palestine presupposes two sovereignties ("you cannot confederate one thing"). CON's own answer to the Ariel question — Palestinian police, Palestinian law, on Palestinian territory, with settlers as residents — confirmed exactly that, and PRO's closing exploited it cleanly: the real comparison became partition-with-a-border versus partition-without, i.e. an intra-motion dispute rather than a rival to the motion. CON's closing accusation that PRO "surrendered the content" is rhetorically strong but does not defeat the claim that CON's plan is itself a two-state outcome, and CON never showed its own rival clears the achievability bar it demands (no constituency in either society, Palestinian acceptance of 700,000 resident settlers unaddressed, same Knesset recognition vote). PRO also neutralized the polling attack with the "least bad anticipates unpopularity" move. Minor cost to PRO: it asserted CON's Ariel answer "never came" when CON had not yet had the chance to reply, and it was clipped more often. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's absorption of CON's alternative — "confederation presupposes two sovereignties; you cannot confederate one thing" — combined with CON's own answer that a settler in Ariel would be arrested by Palestinian police under Palestinian law. That exchange converted CON's rival into a version of the motion, and CON's counter (the defining feature is the hard border) read as narrowing the motion rather than defeating it.</best_rebuttal>
